source_text: Horum igitur tempora obseruantes et dies et menses et annos galaticamur? plane, si Iudaicarum caeremoniarum, si legalium sollemnitatum obseruantes sumus; illas enim apostolus dedocet compescens ueteris testamenti in Christo sepulti perseuerantiam et noui sistens. quod si noua conditio in Christo, noua et sollemnia esse debebunt: aut si omnem in totum deuotionem temporum et dierum et mensium et annorum erasit apostolus, cur pascha celebramus annuo circulo in mense primo? cur quinquaginta exinde diebus in omni exultatione decurrimus? cur stationibus quartam et sextam sabbati dicamus et ieiuniis parasceuen? quamquam uos etiam sabbatum, si quando, continuatis, numquam nisi in pascha ieiunandum secundum rationem alibi redditam. nobis certe omnis dies etiam uulgata consecratione celebratur. nec ergo apud apostolum differentiae ratio, distinguentem noua et uetera. sed et hic inaequalitas uestra ridebitur, cum uetustatum formam nobis exprobratis in quo causam nouitatis accusatis.
thought_title: New observances for a new condition in Christ
orientation: Tertullian is answering the objection that observing times, days, months, and years makes his group guilty of the Galatian error, by arguing that the apostle abolished only Jewish and old-covenant observances, not all devotional times.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore, observing the times of these things and days and months and years, are we acting like the Galatians? Clearly, if we are observers of Jewish ceremonies, if of legal solemnities; for the apostle unteaches those things, checking the persistence of the old testament buried in Christ and establishing the new. But if the condition in Christ is new, the solemnities also will have to be new: or if the apostle scraped away every devotion of times and days and months and years entirely, why do we celebrate the Passover in a yearly cycle in the first month? Why do we run through the fifty days from then on in all exultation? Why do we assign Wednesday and Friday to station fasts and the Preparation Day to fastings? Although you also sometimes continue the Sabbath, never is there to be fasting except at Passover according to the reason given elsewhere. For us certainly every day is celebrated even by common consecration. Therefore there is not among the apostle a reason of distinction, distinguishing new things and old things. But here also your inconsistency will be laughed at, when you reproach us with the form of old things in the very matter in which you accuse the cause of newness.

choices.english: are we acting like the Galatians
choices.why: The verb is coined from Galatia and means to imitate the Galatians' error of observing times; rendering as a verb phrase keeps the rhetorical question's force.

choices.term: ueteris testamenti in Christo sepulti perseuerantiam
choices.english: the persistence of the old testament buried in Christ
choices.why: Keeps the genitive chain and the metaphor of burial, which is central to Tertullian's argument that the old covenant is dead and buried.
rejected: the old testament's persistence, buried in Christ
the persistence of the old covenant that was buried in Christ

choices.english: the condition in Christ is new
choices.why: Conditio means legal status or condition; rendering as 'condition' preserves the legal flavor of the argument about old versus new covenant.

choices.english: the fourth and sixth day of the week
choices.why: Sabbati here means 'of the week' in Jewish reckoning; the glossary's stationes are Wednesday and Friday, so the literal rendering clarifies the days.
rejected: the fourth and sixth of the Sabbath

choices.why: Uulgata means widespread or common; the phrase contrasts the opponents' limited holy days with the New Prophecy's view that every day is consecrated.
Uetustatum is plural genitive of uetustas, meaning oldness or old practices; 'form of old things' keeps the plural and the charge of antiquated practice.

bible_refs.note: You observe days and months and seasons and years

pass_b_english: So when we observe times and days and months and years, are we behaving like the Galatians? Certainly, if we are observing Jewish ceremonies and legal solemnities. For the apostle unteaches those things. He checks the persistence of the old testament buried in Christ and establishes the new. But if the condition in Christ is new, then new solemnities ought to exist as well. Or if the apostle scraped away every devotion of times and days and months and years entirely, why do we celebrate Passover in an annual cycle in the first month? Why do we run through the fifty days after it in all exultation? Why do we dedicate Wednesday and Friday to station fasts, and the Preparation Day to fastings? Although you also sometimes keep the Sabbath unbroken, you say that one must never fast except at Passover, according to the reasoning given elsewhere. For us, certainly, every day is celebrated even by common consecration. So there is no reasoning of distinction with the apostle, who distinguishes new and old. But here too your inconsistency will be laughed at, when you reproach us with the form of old things in the very matter where you accuse the cause of newness.

last_rejected.quote: you say that one must never fast except at Passover
last_rejected.source_quote: numquam nisi in pascha ieiunandum secundum rationem alibi redditam
last_rejected.why: 'secundum rationem alibi redditam' means 'according to the reasoning given elsewhere,' but the English attaches it to the opponents' statement rather than Tertullian's cross-reference; also 'you say' adds agency not in source.
last_rejected.fix: you never fast except at Passover, according to the reasoning given elsewhere
last_rejected.ruling: Latin implies 'you' (vos) and 'according to the reasoning given elsewhere' modifies the fasting rule, matching English rendering.

last_rejected.quote: For the apostle unteaches those things, checking the persistence...
last_rejected.source_quote: illās enim apostolus dedocet compescens veteris testamenti in Christo sepulti perseuerantiam et novī sistens.
last_rejected.why: Latin says the apostle teaches (dedocet), not unteaches; the English adds a negation, reversing the meaning.
last_rejected.fix: For the apostle teaches those things, restraining the perseverance of the old testament buried in Christ and establishing the new.
last_rejected.ruling: dedocet means 'unteaches' or 'teaches against'; English correctly captures the apostle opposing those practices.

polish.changed: Clarified 'the Preparation Day' as Friday, smoothed sentence order, and made the apostle's two actions distinct for easier reading aloud.

notes.why: Reader may not know this is Friday.

problems.quote: the fourth feria and the sixth
problems.why: 'Feria' is Latin for weekday; 'fourth feria' = Wednesday, 'sixth' = Friday. Reader may not connect terms.

variants.text: the fourth feria and the sixth
the fourth and sixth days of the week

problems.quote: the fourth feria and the sixth
problems.why: Same days named differently; 'feria' is unexplained Latin.
problems.fix: Translate 'feria' as 'day' or explain it on first use.

problems.why: 'Fastings' appears as variant of 'station fasts' without explanation.
problems.fix: Use 'station fasts' consistently or explain the variant.

edits.old: Why do we dedicate the fourth and sixth day of the week to station fasts, and Friday to fastings?
edits.new: Why do we dedicate Wednesday and Friday to station fasts, and the Preparation Day to fastings?

fixed: The English 'the fourth and sixth day of the week' is understandable but the glossary flags 'feria' as unexplained Latin; the source 'quartam et sextam sabbati' means the fourth and sixth day of the week, which in Christian usage are Wednesday and Friday. Replaced with the day names for clarity.

The English 'Friday to fastings' misstates the source: 'parasceuen' is the Preparation Day (Friday before the Sabbath), not simply 'Friday'. The source distinguishes station fasts on Wednesday and Friday from fastings on the Preparation Day. Restored 'the Preparation Day' to match the source.
The gloss 'the fourth and sixth day of the week' was flagged as unclear; replaced with 'Wednesday and Friday' to match the edited English.
